title: On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music (trans. A. J. Ellis; German orig. 1863)
key_findings: Founding text of physiological acoustics: German original 1863; Ellis English translation 1875 (from 3rd German ed.), revised 1885 (4th ed.); 1895 reprint on archive.org (public domain)
practical_applications: Historical anchor for timbre-as-harmonics and roughness/beats as the basis of dissonance
limitations: Existence and edition history confirmed; content not re-read this session; resonance-place theory later superseded in detail

title: Loudness, Its Definition, Measurement and Calculation
key_findings: Defines loudness level of any sound as the intensity level of an equally loud 1000 Hz reference tone (listener facing a small source, both ears)

Argues loudness is psychological: if it depended only on intensity, physical measurement would determine it; measured loudness levels of pure tones and complex sounds to build an empirical loudness formula
First equal-loudness contours (the 'Fletcher-Munson curves'); later redeterminations (Churcher & King 1937, Robinson & Dadson 1956) led to ISO 226
practical_applications: Explains why mixes sound bass-thin at low playback level
limitations: 1930s headphone/equipment calibration; superseded numerically by ISO 226:2023

title: On the psychophysical law
key_findings: Revived the power law (sensation = k * stimulus^n) from magnitude-estimation data; loudness is a 'prothetic' (Class I) continuum where JNDs grow in subjective size up the scale
Secondary sources list loudness exponent ~0.67 re sound pressure (about 0.3 re intensity) for a 3 kHz tone: +10 dB is roughly a doubling of loudness (sone scale)
practical_applications: A 10 dB cut sounds like 'half as loud', not 'a bit quieter' -> plan ducking depth in dB with that in mind
limitations: Method critiqued: averaging across observers then fitting a power function does not directly test the law; exponents context-dependent

title: Subdivision of the Audible Frequency Range into Critical Bands (Frequenzgruppen)
key_findings: Tabulated 24 critical bands (Bark scale 1-24); bands roughly 100 Hz wide below ~500 Hz, roughly proportional (log-like) above (per secondary sources)
practical_applications: Masking and loudness summation work per critical band: sounds in the same band fight; spreading sounds across bands raises loudness without raising level
limitations: Content via secondary sources (Wikipedia, Siemens KB); later ERB scale (Glasberg & Moore 1990) is the modern alternative

title: Auditory Scene Analysis: The Perceptual Organization of Sound
key_findings: Founded auditory scene analysis: the brain groups sound elements into 'streams' (one per source) by sequential and simultaneous integration; alternating tones split into two streams when far apart in pitch/fast
MIT Press 1990 (pb 1994); companion audio demonstrations with P. Ahad
practical_applications: Make VO a separate 'stream' from music: different register, timbre, location (centre), onset timing
limitations: Book content summarised from secondary pages; McGill site being discontinued

title: ISO 226:2023 Acoustics - Normal equal-loudness-level contours
key_findings: 3rd edition (2023-03): contours for pure tones, one-third-octave frequencies 20 Hz-12.5 kHz, otologically normal listeners aged 18-25, frontal free progressive plane wave, binaural
Differs from 2003 edition by up to 0.6 dB (improved loudness model); 20 Hz values changed with ISO 389-7:2019
practical_applications: Judge balance at moderate level and check low level; low and very high frequencies need more level to sound equally loud
limitations: Pure tones, young listeners only - not broadband programme or older/hearing-impaired audiences

title: Recommendation ITU-R BS.1770-5: Algorithms to measure audio programme loudness and true-peak audio level
key_findings: Loudness = K-weighting (stage 1 shelving filter modelling the head, stage 2 RLB high-pass) -> mean square per channel -> channel-weighted sum (LFE excluded) -> gating
True-peak measured by oversampling + interpolation (secondary source: x4 oversampler) because peaks can fall between samples
practical_applications: LUFS approximates perceived loudness of whole programmes; dBTP guards against inter-sample clipping after codecs
limitations: ITU PDF blocked to our client this session; details from search snippets; K-weighting is a simple model, not a full loudness model (no masking, no ISO 226 shape)

title: EBU R 128: Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals (v4.0, 2020)
key_findings: Recommends Programme Loudness (gated per BS.1770, i.e. foreground loudness) for normalisation and Maximum True Peak for headroom; peak normalisation causes loudness jumps
Max Momentary / Short-term loudness (Tech 3341) may be used to check upper tolerance; Loudness Range not recommended for programmes under 1 minute (based on 3 s short-term values)
Relative gate changed from -8 to -10 LU (2010)
practical_applications: For Reels/TikTok (<60 s) do not trust LRA; use short-term max to catch loud SFX moments
limitations: Broadcast target -23 LUFS not used by social platforms

title: EBU Tech 3341: Loudness Metering 'EBU Mode' metering to supplement EBU R 128
key_findings: Three time scales: Momentary (0.4 s sliding window, ungated), Short-term (3 s window, ungated), Integrated (gated)
Gating: absolute -70 LUFS 'silence' gate, then relative gate 10 LU below absolute-gated level, on 400 ms blocks with 75% overlap; 1 LU = 1 dB; LRA unstable in first 60 s
practical_applications: Silent pauses do not lower Integrated loudness much (gated) -> designed silence is 'free' in LUFS terms
limitations: Meter spec, not a perception study

title: EBU R37-2007: The relative timing of the sound and vision components of a television signal
key_findings: End-to-end limits at emission: sound may lead picture by at most 40 ms and lag by at most 60 ms
Per-stage accuracy: 5 ms early to 15 ms late; values from subjective tests where lip-sync failure becomes perceptible to 50% of observers; HD needs extra care
practical_applications: Our render chain should keep VO-to-mouth offset inside +40/-60 ms; prefer sound slightly late over early
limitations: Broadcast viewing conditions (EBU R28); 50% detection threshold, so sensitive viewers notice smaller errors

title: Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Standard reference for masking, critical bands, loudness (sone), roughness, sharpness; secondary sources cite: forward (post-) masking lasts up to ~200 ms after masker end, backward (pre-) masking only ~5-20 ms
practical_applications: A loud hit can hide the first ~100-200 ms of a following word -> leave a gap after big SFX before VO
limitations: Book not read; temporal-masking durations taken from search summaries of papers citing it; values vary with level and method

title: Hearing lips and seeing voices
key_findings: Audio [ba] dubbed onto lip movements of [ga] was reported as [da] by most adults; reverse dubbing gave [bagba]/[gaba]; audio alone or undubbed film identified correctly
practical_applications: Mouth shapes of a talking character change what syllable is heard -> lip-sync shapes matter, especially for closed-lip consonants (b/p/m)
limitations: Effect size varies greatly across individuals, languages and stimuli; later work shows weaker effect in some language groups

title: Temporal window of integration in auditory-visual speech perception
authors: Virginie van Wassenhove; Ken W. Grant; David Poeppel
key_findings: 43 normal-hearing participants; McGurk fusion persisted from about -30 ms (audio lead) to +170 ms (audio lag) across asynchronies tested from -467 to +467 ms
Simultaneity and fusion windows similar: an asymmetric ~200 ms audio-visual integration window favouring visual lead
practical_applications: Speech can be up to ~1-4 frames late and still fuse, but only ~1 frame early
limitations: Syllables in lab; abstract only

title: The ventriloquist effect results from near-optimal bimodal integration
key_findings: When visual localisation is good, vision captures sound location; with heavily blurred visuals, sound captures vision; at intermediate blur perception follows the reliability-weighted mean (MLE); bimodal precision better than either sense (6 subjects)
practical_applications: Mono phone speaker sound is 'pulled' to the on-screen source -> no need to pan for location; whichever sense is more reliable dominates
limitations: Small n, simple blobs and clicks; full text PDF blocked (403) to our client

title: Crossmodal correspondences: A tutorial review
key_findings: Crossmodal correspondences (e.g. high pitch <-> small, bright, high in space) act as a constraint on crossmodal binding alongside spatial, temporal and semantic congruency

Three classes: structural (e.g. loudness-brightness; possibly innate, from neural coding of magnitude), statistical (pitch-elevation, pitch-size, loudness-size; learned from environmental regularities), semantic (via shared words like 'high/low'; emerge with language)
Effects show in speeded classification (faster when congruent) and in integration; children match loud sounds with large shapes by age 2
practical_applications: Map sound to visual size/brightness/height consistently: small bright thing = higher, brighter sound; big heavy = lower
limitations: Some correspondences relative not absolute; semantic ones language-dependent

title: 'When Birds of a Feather Flock Together': Synesthetic Correspondences Modulate Audiovisual Integration in Non-Synesthetes
key_findings: Three experiments: pitch-size (temporal), pitch/waveform-shape (angular star with high/square tone vs curvy with low), pitch-size (spatial; 300 Hz vs 4500 Hz tones, 12 participants in Exp 3)
Temporal order and spatial discrepancy judgments were less precise for congruent pairs -> congruent pairs are integrated more strongly (first psychophysical evidence)
practical_applications: A sound that 'matches' the object's size/shape fuses with it better and hides small sync errors
limitations: Correspondences likely relative to the stimulus set; lab stimuli

title: The bouba/kiki effect is robust across cultures and writing systems
key_findings: Online experiment, speakers of 25 languages, 9 families, 10 writing systems: strong overall effect; bouba gave more congruent responses than kiki
Roman-script users only marginally more likely to show the effect; not stronger where letter shapes match -> rooted in voice-shape correspondence, largely independent of orthography
practical_applications: Round soft shapes <-> rounded voiced sounds (b, m, o, u); spiky <-> k, t, i - for naming, SFX and logo motion
limitations: Online sample, pseudowords; strength varies by language

title: Music-color associations are mediated by emotion
authors: Stephen E. Palmer; Karen B. Schloss; Zoe Xu; Lilia R. Prado-Leon
key_findings: US and Mexican participants matched colours to 18 classical pieces: faster major-mode music -> lighter, more saturated, yellower; slower minor -> darker, desaturated, bluer
Emotional associations of music and chosen colours correlated 0.89 < r < 0.99 in both cultures; same pattern for faces
practical_applications: Pick grade/palette and music together by shared emotion: upbeat track + warm saturated light; slow minor + desaturated blue
limitations: Western classical music only; two cultures; later work suggests synaesthetes map differently

title: Commercializing Sonic Seasoning in Multisensory Offline Experiential Events and Online Tasting Experiences
authors: Charles Spence; Qian Janice Wang; Felipe Reinoso-Carvalho; Steve Keller
key_findings: Defines sonic seasoning (deliberate sound-taste pairing); reviews ~30 brand activations 2011-2021

Measured cases are few: The Singleton Sensorium 2013 (~500 guests; grassiness rated higher in 'grassy' sound room); Courvoisier 2013 only partly matched composer intent; most activations (Beck's Frequency 2020 Cannes Lions etc.) report no taste evidence
Effects strongest when sound comes before/during tasting; background noise can harm taste
practical_applications: Use crossmodal sound as a supporting cue, test it, never claim a measured effect without data
limitations: Narrative review relying on press/brand reports; one author works for an audio agency; read first ~40% of the page text

title: Timbre and affect dimensions: Evidence from affect and similarity ratings and acoustic correlates of isolated instrument sounds
authors: Tuomas Eerola; Rafael Ferrer; Vinoo Alluri
key_findings: 110 then 105 isolated instrument sounds (same pitch, duration, dynamics) rated reliably on valence and energy arousal; 50-57% of variance predicted by few acoustic features

Valence correlated r = -.74 with ratio of high- to low-frequency energy (brighter/sharper = less pleasant); attack slope and spectral flux tied to energy arousal; preference and valence nearly identical (r = .97)
practical_applications: Soft attack + darker spectrum = calmer, more pleasant (eye-break, heartwarming); bright fast-attack = energetic/edgy (beat clips, alerts)
limitations: Isolated Western instrument tones, not mixes or voices; correlational

title: Human Screams Occupy a Privileged Niche in the Communication Soundscape
authors: Luc H. Arnal; Adeen Flinker; Andreas Kleinschmidt; Anne-Lise Giraud; David Poeppel
key_findings: Screams carry fast amplitude modulation ~30-150 Hz ('roughness') unused by normal speech (~4-5 Hz modulation); rougher sounds rated more frightening and increased amygdala response
Artificial alarms and dissonant intervals also fall in the roughness range
practical_applications: Roughness = alarm/fear tool: use for horror/zombie, never under calm VO or eye-break clips
limitations: Read via Max Planck press release; lab ratings

title: Rising Sound Intensity: An Intrinsic Warning Cue Activating the Amygdala
authors: Dominik R. Bach; Hartmut Schaechinger; John G. Neuhoff; et al.
key_findings: Rising vs falling intensity sounds: rising facilitates autonomic orienting and phasic alertness; activates amygdala plus intraparietal sulcus, STS and temporal plane (event-related fMRI)
practical_applications: Crescendo/riser = attention grab; a fade-in is not neutral
limitations: Lab tones; a 2015 follow-up: rising intensity read as approach only for complex (not white-noise) carriers

title: Neural mechanisms of involuntary attention to acoustic novelty and change
authors: Carles Escera; Kimmo Alho; Istvan Winkler; Risto Naatanen
key_findings: Irrelevant novel sounds (10%) slowed responses to a visual task by 17 ms vs standard tones; slightly deviant tones (10%) lowered hit rate
Two mechanisms: transient detector (N1) for novel onsets and change detector (MMN ~150 ms; P3a 230/315 ms) for deviance
practical_applications: Unexpected sound onsets pull attention involuntarily -> powerful for hooks, costly when they interrupt reading of on-screen text
limitations: Lab oddball paradigm; small ms effects

title: The evolution of the Lombard effect: 100 years of psychoacoustic research
key_findings: Centenary review of noise-dependent vocal amplitude regulation (Lombard effect) in humans and animals; may be >300 million years old if shared by all amniotes
practical_applications: Speech recorded or synthesised as if in quiet sounds 'wrong' over loud music; a slightly raised, clearer delivery suits noisy scenes
limitations: Review of vocal production, not of listener benefit; abstract only

title: Development of a quick speech-in-noise test for measuring signal-to-noise ratio loss in normal-hearing and hearing-impaired listeners
authors: Mead C. Killion; Patricia A. Niquette; Gail I. Gudmundsen; Lawrence J. Revit; Shilpi Banerjee
key_findings: QuickSIN measures the SNR needed for 50% key words in four-talker babble; SNRs 25 to 0 dB; single-list SD 1.4 dB for hearing-impaired; accuracy +/-2.7 dB (95%)
Secondary (canadianaudiologist): normal hearing needs about +2 dB SNR for 50% words; SNR loss = extra dB a listener needs
practical_applications: 50% words is far from comfortable; for easy listening aim many dB above that (VO 10-20 dB over bed)
limitations: Babble masker in English; clinical test not media mix target

title: More than a feeling: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR) is characterized by reliable changes in affect and physiology
authors: Giulia Lara Poerio; Emma Blakey; Thomas J. Hostler; Theresa Veltri
key_findings: Study 1 online (ASMR n=813, non-ASMR n=189), Study 2 lab (55 + 55): ASMR videos raised pleasant affect only in people who experience ASMR
Lab: ASMR group heart rate fell on average 3.41 bpm (d = 0.39) and skin conductance rose 0.30 uS - relaxing yet arousing (excitement, connectedness)
practical_applications: Whisper/close-mic textures work only for a subset of viewers; never rely on them as the only calming device
limitations: Self-selected experiencers; modest effects; short exposure

title: Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR): a flow-like mental state
authors: Emma L. Barratt; Nick J. Davis
key_findings: Online survey of 475 self-identified experiencers: triggers whispering 75%, personal attention 69%, crisp sounds 64%, slow movements 53%; 98% use for relaxation, 82% for sleep, 81% watch before sleep; many prefer binaural headphones
Synaesthesia prevalence 5.9% in sample; temporary relief of depression/chronic pain symptoms self-reported
practical_applications: Calm clip triggers: soft close sounds, slow movement, personal address; quiet listening context
limitations: Self-selected online sample, self-report, correlational

title: Autonomous sensory meridian response (ASMR): A PRISMA-guided systematic review
authors: Tobias Lohaus; Sarah C. Schreckenberg; Silja Bellingrath; Patrizia Thoma
key_findings: Systematic review (search to March 2022) of 54 quantitative studies; physiological changes such as heart-rate reduction; many studies small and low-diversity; no study shows long-term mental-health effects (per press release)
practical_applications: Treat ASMR calm as short-term and audience-dependent
limitations: Read via press release only; online-first Nov 2023, print vol. 12(4) 2025

title: Cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, and respiratory changes induced by different types of music in musicians and non-musicians: the importance of silence
authors: Luciano Bernardi; Cesare Porta; Peter Sleight
key_findings: 12 musicians + 12 controls; six styles with a random 2-min pause: faster tempo and simpler rhythm raised ventilation, BP and HR; the pause reduced HR, BP and minute ventilation even below baseline
Musicians more respiration-sensitive to tempo; no habituation
practical_applications: Silence after sound is a relaxation tool: build pauses into calm clips instead of continuous music
limitations: n = 24, young healthy, Western music; physiological not emotional ratings

title: World report on hearing (news release 'WHO: 1 in 4 people projected to have hearing problems by 2050')
key_findings: 2 March 2021: nearly 2.5 billion people (1 in 4) projected to have some hearing loss by 2050; at least 700 million will need ear/hearing care; report states >1.5 billion now, 430 million moderate or worse (secondary)
practical_applications: Design every clip for imperfect hearing: captions, high VO-to-bed ratio, no information carried only by sound
limitations: Global projections; definitions of 'hearing loss' vary

title: Hearing health survey of the population in Bangkok
authors: Suwimol Ruencharoen; Krisna Lertsukprasert; Ravin Suvanich; et al.
key_findings: Random survey of 2,463 Bangkok adults aged 15-96 with pure-tone audiometry: hearing loss (any >25 dB HL) 53.02%, rising with age; moderate or worse 2.8%; 65+ had 8.56x odds; men 2x; >8 h/day noise work 1.56x
practical_applications: Thai audiences include many mild-loss listeners -> clear VO, captions
limitations: Bangkok only; 'any frequency >25 dB HL' is a broad definition

title: The effective screening tools for detecting hearing loss in elderly population: HHIE-ST Versus TSQ
authors: Nichtima Chayaopas; Pornthep Kasemsiri; Panida Thanawirattananit; Patorn Piromchai; Kwanchanok Yimtae
key_findings: 1,109 Thai adults aged 60+ in four (north-eastern) provinces, audiometry 250-8000 Hz as gold standard: hearing disability prevalence 38.34%
practical_applications: Older Thai viewers (presbyopia/eyewear audience) often have hearing disability -> design VO and captions for them
limitations: Regional community sample; screening-tool study

title: Age-Related Differences of Mandarin Tone and Consonant Aspiration Perception in Babble Noise
authors: Yaru Meng; Fei Chen; Feng Yan; Gang Peng; Wei Zheng
key_findings: 24 adults + 20 adolescents: in babble, consonant aspiration categorisation degraded more than tone perception; tone perception more robust to noise
practical_applications: For tonal languages (Thai by analogy, unverified) the fragile part in noise is consonants, i.e. the 2-8 kHz detail -> keep that band clear of music
limitations: Mandarin, not Thai; no direct Thai speech-in-noise study found this session

title: Video Captions Benefit Everyone
key_findings: More than 100 empirical studies: same-language captions improve comprehension of, attention to and memory for video; biggest benefits for non-native viewers, learners to read, D/deaf and hard-of-hearing
Captions also carry sound effects ('footsteps approaching') and speaker identity; ASR captions not yet error-free
practical_applications: Burn-in captions for VO clips; caption key SFX in story clips for sound-off viewers
limitations: Critique (WatsonLB): evidence base leans on L2, non-neurotypical and self-report studies; 'everyone' overstated for neurotypical native viewers

title: Verizon Media and Publicis Media survey on captions and sound-off viewing (reported by 3Play Media / MarketingCharts)
authors: Verizon Media; Publicis Media (reported by 3Play Media)
key_findings: Online survey of 5,616 US adults 18-54, April 2019: 69% watch video with sound off in public places, 25% in private (secondary: Kapwing, MarketingCharts); 80% more likely to finish a captioned video (secondary)
3Play page: 41% of videos incomprehensible without sound; 80% of caption users are not D/deaf or hard of hearing (citing Ofcom)
practical_applications: Every clip must make sense on mute: text layer + captions + visual storytelling
limitations: Industry-commissioned survey, US only, self-report; numbers relayed by vendors; not Thailand

title: Evolution of Sound, Volume 1 (TikTok for Business blog, 21 Dec 2021)
key_findings: 88% of users say sound is vital to the TikTok experience (Nielsen Marketing Science US Authenticity Study, July 2020); Kantar cross-platform sound research Jan 2021: brand awareness lifts for sound-on ads
practical_applications: TikTok is sound-on by culture; Reels/FB feeds are more often muted -> design for both
limitations: Platform-commissioned, self-interested, no sample sizes; contradicts sound-off surveys because of platform and setting

title: Understanding Success Criterion 1.4.7: Low or No Background Audio (WCAG 2.2, Level AAA)
key_findings: Prerecorded speech-foreground audio: no background, or background can be turned off, or background at least 20 dB below foreground speech; sounds of 1-2 s exempt; intent: hard-of-hearing users separate speech from background
practical_applications: Accessibility version of a clip: bed >= 20 dB under VO (stricter than the 10 LU Torcoli minimum)
limitations: Written for audio-only web content; dB measurement method loosely specified

title: Loud Commercials / CALM Act (Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation Act)
key_findings: Enacted 15 Dec 2010 after consumer complaints about loud ads; FCC rules effective 13 Dec 2012 adopt ATSC A/85: a commercial's average loudness must not exceed the programme's; no absolute cap; A/85:2013 adds gating; FCC 25-16 (2025) notes an uptick in complaints in 2024
practical_applications: Documented failure of 'louder sells': regulators had to force loudness parity
limitations: Read via search snippets (FCC site 403 to our client)

title: Bass extension of microspeaker system on mobile device
authors: J. R. Chang; C. N. Wang
key_findings: In a 10-inch tablet, a front chamber + pipe port extended the microspeaker's low-frequency limit from 630 Hz to 300 Hz
practical_applications: Even good mobile speakers reproduce little below ~300-600 Hz: bass-only cues (sub drops, kick fundamentals) vanish on phone speakers; carry weight with harmonics/mid-range
limitations: One device design paper, not a survey of handsets; patents found cite ~1 kHz microspeaker resonance and steep roll-off below ~300 Hz (not peer reviewed)

title: Press coverage of 'inaudible dialogue' complaints about Christopher Nolan's Interstellar (2014) and Tenet (2020)
authors: Various (Yahoo/The Playlist/RedShark News; Nolan quoted from T. Shone 'The Nolan Variations' and THR 2014)
key_findings: Viewers and critics reported dialogue buried under music/effects in Tenet; Nolan said other filmmakers called to complain and defended the mix as a deliberate choice ('right approach for an experimental film', on Interstellar, THR 2014)
practical_applications: Case of deliberate low intelligibility: an aesthetic choice that a mass mobile audience will read as an error
limitations: Press/anecdotal; attribution of quotes between films unclear in coverage
